lead: Three cheap operations shrink a token list before a model reads it. Stemming cuts endings by fixed rules, so cats becomes cat. Lemmatization returns the dictionary base form and needs a part of speech, so ran becomes run. Stop-word removal deletes very frequent tokens such as the and was. The aim is a smaller, denser vocabulary; the risk is losing meaning.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.4 for the token list that this chapter reduces.

blocks.text: A token is one occurrence of a word in running text. A word form is the exact string of that occurrence. The distinct strings in a corpus form its vocabulary, also called its types. A news corpus of a million running words has a few tens of thousands of types, and most are rare inflections of common words.

A stem is what is left after mechanical suffix stripping. It is a string, not necessarily an English word: studies gives studi. A lemma is the dictionary headword. It is always a real word and is tied to a part of speech: the lemma of studies is study.

Stemming is fast and crude; lemmatization is slower, needs a lexicon and a tag, and gives the right base form when the tag is right. Both cut the vocabulary and merge counts of related forms. Neither is reversible: from studi you cannot tell whether the source was studies or studied.
A stemmer is a fixed program, not a trained model. The Porter stemmer is the standard teaching example: it pushes the word through steps, each holding a list of suffixes.

items: Set the current string to the input word.
At each step, compare the string with that step's suffix rules, longest suffix first.
Apply the first rule whose suffix matches and whose condition on the remaining stem is true; if none matches, go to the next step.
After the last step, return the string.

blocks.text: m = number of VC sequences in C(VC)ᵐV
blocks.where: m is the measure of a stem. C is a consonant letter, V a vowel letter, and the bracket repeats m times. If a word ends in a consonant after the last V, treat a V as following: cat = CVC is treated as CVCV. m counts vowel-then-consonant pairs after the first consonant run. cat has m = 1; better (CVCCVC) has m = 2.

items: Step 1a, ies → i: ponies becomes poni, lies becomes li.
Step 1a: delete a final s only when the part before it contains a vowel not immediately before the s: cats becomes cat; gas stays gas; was stays was.
Step 1a, sses → ss: classes becomes class.

blocks.text: Lovins' stemmer, one of the earliest, matched a long table of endings, each with its own context condition. The Lancaster stemmer strips endings until no rule matches, so its stems are shorter and rougher.

Errors run two ways. Over-stemming merges words of different meaning: university and universe both reduce to univers. Under-stemming leaves related forms apart: lies becomes li while lie stays lie, so two forms of one lemma never meet.

sections.h3: Lemmatization: the dictionary form needs a tag

blocks.text: Lemmatization asks which headword a word form belongs to. The answer depends on part of speech, so the input is a pair of word form and POS tag, not a bare string. A lexicon or a morphological analyser supplies the mapping; Chapter 1.6 builds one with a finite-state transducer.
Saw as a verb is the past tense of see; saw as a noun is the headword saw. Feed the wrong tag and you get the wrong lemma.

The stemmer leaves better and happily nearly untouched and can never cross an irregular form. The lemmatizer returns real words, so better maps to good. The price is speed and data: a lemmatizer needs a tagger, a lexicon and language rules, while a stemmer needs one file of suffix rules.

sections.h3: Stop words: dropping the frequent and empty

blocks.text: A stop word is a token so frequent that it says little about topic. Articles, prepositions, auxiliaries and pronouns fill the top of every frequency list: the, a, of, is, was, and, to. A stop list is a set of such strings, and removal deletes every token in the set before counting.

List length is a design choice. Published English lists run from about 100 to a few hundred entries, and no single list suits all work. The list depends on the domain: patient says little in general text but is central in clinical notes, and an engine that drops the cannot answer a query about the band The Who. Build the list from your own frequency counts and read the top 100 by hand.

Negation is the dangerous case. Once not is deleted, not good and good become the same bag of words, so a sentiment system reads a negative review as positive. Keep not, no, never and none whenever the task depends on polarity. Other pipelines keep all stop words and let weighting such as TF-IDF, see Unit 5, push them down.

Removal shortens documents and shrinks the vocabulary, which speeds training and reduces sparsity. It also throws away word order and negation cues, so accuracy can fall. Measure both effects on your own task rather than trusting a default list.

examples.question: A pipeline receives the token list [cats, cat, ran, run, the, was, lies, lie]. The stop list is {the, was}. Apply Porter step 1a (ies → i, and delete a final s only when the preceding part contains a vowel not immediately before the s), and take lemmas from a dictionary. (a) How many distinct word forms, stems and lemmas does the input have? (b) How many tokens survive stop-word removal, and how many distinct stems and lemmas do they have? (c) How many characters does stemming remove from the survivors?
steps: the and was are in the stop list and are deleted. Six tokens survive: cats, cat, ran, run, lies, lie.
cats → cat: the part before the s, cat, contains the vowel a, which is not directly before the s, so the s is deleted, 1 character removed. cat → cat, 0. ran → ran, 0. run → run, 0.
lies ends in ies, so lies → li, 2 characters removed. lie has no final s and does not end in ies, so step 1a leaves it as it is, 0 removed.
Lemmas: cats and cat → cat. ran and run → run. the → the. was → be. lies and lie → lie.
(a) Distinct forms = 8. Distinct stems = {cat, ran, run, the, was, li, lie} = 7. Distinct lemmas = {cat, run, the, be, lie} = 5.
(b) Survivors = 6 tokens. Distinct stems = {cat, ran, run, li, lie} = 5. Distinct lemmas = {cat, run, lie} = 3.
(c) Characters removed = 1 (cats) + 0 + 0 + 0 + 2 (lies) + 0 (lie) = 3. Only li is not a word, which is the price of stemming.
examples.answer: 8 forms, 7 stems and 5 lemmas in the input; 6 tokens, 5 stems and 3 lemmas after stop-word removal; stemming removes 3 characters from the survivors.

print(len({stem[t] for t in kept}))
print(len({lemma[t] for t in kept}))
print(sum(len(t) - len(stem[t]) for t in kept))

traps: Printing a stem to a user: studi and li are not English words, so stems belong inside the index, never on screen.
Deleting not or never before sentiment analysis: not good and good collapse to the same bag of words and the polarity flips.
Running a lemmatizer without a part of speech: saw as a verb gives see, saw as a noun gives saw, so the tagger must run first.
Assuming stemming and lemmatization agree: better stems to better but lemmatizes to good.
Believing a longer stop list is always better: the list depends on the domain, and dropping the kills a query about The Who.

quiz.q: Define stem and lemma in one line each.
quiz.a: A stem is the string left after mechanical suffix stripping and need not be a word. A lemma is the dictionary headword of a word form, always a real word and tied to a part of speech.

quiz.q: In the Porter stemmer, what does the measure m count, and what is m for better?
quiz.a: m counts vowel-consonant sequences in the stem. Better is C V C C V C, which has two VC sequences, so m = 2.

quiz.q: Why can a lemmatizer not run on a bare word list?
quiz.a: The lemma depends on part of speech: saw is the past of see as a verb and the headword saw as a noun. Without a tag the analyser must guess, so the pipeline tags first, then lemmatizes.

quiz.q: Apply Porter step 1a (ies → i, and delete a final s only when the preceding part contains a vowel not immediately before the s) to ponies, cats and gas. Give each stem and the characters removed.
quiz.a: ponies → poni, 2 removed. cats → cat, 1 removed. gas → gas, 0 removed: the vowel a is immediately before the s, so the s stays.

quiz.q: The tokens are [not, good, the, movie]. Give the tokens kept with the stop list {the}, then with {the, not}.
quiz.a: With {the}: not, good, movie, so 3 tokens. With {the, not}: good, movie, so 2 tokens, and the negation a sentiment model needs is gone.

quiz.q: For lies → li and lie → lie, say whether the stemmer over-stems or under-stems, and what that does to a search index.
quiz.a: It under-stems: two forms of one lemma map to different strings, so counts stay split and a query for lie misses lies. The stem li is also not a word, so it can never be shown to a user.

quiz.q: A team deletes 300 stop words, retrains a sentiment classifier and sees accuracy fall. Give two causes and one fix.
quiz.a: Cause one: negation words were removed, so not good reads as good. Cause two: words frequent in this domain but topic-bearing were removed. Fix: build the list from in-domain frequencies, keep negation and contrast words, and leave the rest to TF-IDF weighting.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern neural pipelines rarely stem; they split words into subword pieces with byte-pair encoding or WordPiece, which handles unseen and agglutinative words without a suffix table. Search engines still stem because recall matters more than clean words there. Indian languages with rich inflection, such as Tamil, Telugu or Hindi, gain a lot from a proper morphological analyser rather than a suffix stripper. Search for the Porter stemmer's original description, the Snowball stemming family, and Indic morphological analysers to go further.
